title: Research in the Time of AI
author: Paul Goldsmith-Pinkham
description: Paul Goldsmith-Pinkham (Assistant Professor of Finance, Yale SOM) argues AI tools compress research timelines while preserving what makes research genuinely valuable. Outlines eight research stages (ideation, design, data assembly, analysis, robustness testing, writing, submission, publication) and argues LLMs accelerate transitions between stages but don't eliminate the need for careful iteration. Addresses two central anxieties: (1) "slop" - more papers published faster with less rigor, p-hacking supercharged by automation; and (2) career anxiety - execution skills (coding, writing) now have lower market value. Claude Code features prominently. Key insight: "The hard part is still knowing where to walk." Skills that distinguish good researchers - taste, institutional knowledge, iterative thinking - become more valuable as execution barriers lower.

title: Reflections on Vibe Researching
author: Joshua Gans
description: Joshua Gans conducted a year-long experiment with "AI-first" research ("vibe researching"), using AI at every stage of writing papers in 2025. His conclusion: the experiment ultimately failed. While AI-generated mathematics checked out, theoretical oversights in game theory and equilibrium analysis went undetected until peer review. Reduced friction meant he pursued more mediocre ideas to completion. LLMs present results with false confidence, tempting researchers into believing they've discovered something genuine. Tools used: ChatGPT (o1-pro and 5.2 Pro), Gemini, and Refine.ink. Key takeaway: AI accelerates research substantially but cannot replace human taste, peer judgment, or the value of letting ideas develop naturally. A must-read for academics experimenting with AI in their research process. See also Antonio Mele's response thread.

Finds ~70% of firms actively use AI but report little impact over the past 3 years, while forecasting AI will boost productivity by 1.4% and cut employment by 0.7% over the next 3 years.
highlightDesc: A landmark, representative international benchmark of firm-level AI adoption — a survey of ~6,000 executives across the US, UK, Germany, and Australia by Bloom, Davis, Barrero and co-authors. About 70% of firms report using AI, though self-reported impact so far is small.
shortDescription: First representative international data on firm-level AI use, surveying ~6,000 executives across the US, UK, Germany, and Australia.

title: A.I. and Our Economic Future (NBER)
author: Charles I. Jones
description: Argues that AI may be fundamentally different from prior general-purpose technologies like electricity or semiconductors, because automating intelligence itself has broader effects. Explores the scenario where machines can perform every cognitive and physical task more cheaply than humans and what economics says about that future.
shortDescription: Argues that AI may be fundamentally different from prior general-purpose technologies like electricity or semiconductors, because automating intelligence...

title: What is the impact of AI on productivity?
author: Alex Imas
description: A living document synthesizing all available studies and data on AI's productivity impact. Reviews the disconnect between micro studies (which overwhelmingly find positive effects, especially for low-skill workers) and macro evidence (which is now beginning to show aggregate gains). Updated regularly as new evidence arrives.
shortDescription: A living document synthesizing all available studies and data on AI's productivity impact.

title: Research on AI and the labor market is still in the first inning
author: Jed Kolko
description: PIIE survey of the state of AI-and-labor research. Reviews high-profile studies combining AI exposure measures with employment data, noting mixed results and methodological challenges. Highlights that AI may create entirely new occupations, and productivity research shows benefits but with important caveats.
shortDescription: PIIE survey of the state of AI-and-labor research.

title: The Anthropic Economic Index: Economic Primitives
author: Ruth Appel, Maxim Massenkoff, Peter McCrory, Miles McCain, Ryan Heller, Tyler Neylon, Alex Tamkin
description: Introduces five foundational measurements—task complexity, skill level, purpose, AI autonomy, and success—to track AI's economic impacts. Based on privacy-preserving analysis of 2 million conversations. Finds more complex tasks see the largest speed-ups, with college-level tasks sped up 12x.
highlightDesc: A usage-based measurement of how AI is actually used across the economy, built from a privacy-preserving analysis of ~2 million conversations. Defines five economic primitives — task complexity, skill, purpose, autonomy, and success — to track AI's real-world impact.
shortDescription: Introduces five foundational measurements—task complexity, skill level, purpose, AI autonomy, and success—to track AI's economic impacts.

title: Stata MCP Server
author: Thomas Monk
description: Brings AI capabilities to Stata through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), enabling Claude and other AI assistants to execute Stata commands, run .do files, and interpret economic data directly from code editors like VS Code and Cursor. Supports paper replication, hypothesis testing, and econometrics learning workflows.
shortDescription: Brings AI capabilities to Stata through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), enabling Claude and other AI assistants to execute Stata commands, run .do files,...

title: Menu Pricing of Large Language Models (arXiv)
author: Dirk Bergemann, Alessandro Bonatti, Alex Smolin
description: Develops a framework for optimal pricing and product design of LLMs, where a provider sells menus of token budgets to users who differ in their valuations across a continuum of tasks. Applies mechanism design theory to the economics of AI services.
shortDescription: Develops a framework for optimal pricing and product design of LLMs, where a provider sells menus of token budgets to users who differ in their valuations...

title: The Adoption of Large Language Models in Economics Research (Economics Letters)
author: Maryam Feyzollahi, Nima Rafizadeh
description: Uses a difference-in-differences framework across 25 leading economics journals over 24 years to measure LLM adoption via linguistic footprints. Finds a 4.76 percentage point increase in LLM-associated terms during 2023–2024, more than doubling from 2.85pp in 2023 to 6.67pp in 2024, documenting rapid integration of language models in economics writing.
shortDescription: Difference-in-differences analysis of LLM adoption across 25 leading economics journals. Evidence on how AI is changing research output.

title: Mapping the Structural Divide: U.S. Universities vs AI Disruption
author: Kyle Saunders
description: Interactive map of 1,556 U.S. universities across two dimensions: institutional resilience and post-college market positioning. Visualizes which schools are structurally positioned to weather demographic decline, fiscal stress, and AI disruption. Built with Claude.
shortDescription: Interactive map of 1,556 U.S. universities showing resilience to AI disruption, demographic decline, and fiscal stress.

title: LLM-Friendly Academic Papers: A Proposal
author: Paul Goldsmith-Pinkham
description: Proposes a standard for making academic papers more accessible to LLMs — bundling papers with an llms.txt orientation file and markdown formatting. Addresses the finding that LLM-generated summaries are nearly five times more likely than human-authored ones to overgeneralize scientific conclusions.
shortDescription: Proposes bundling papers with llms.txt files and markdown so AI can better understand research limitations and scope.

title: When Will the Research Paper Disappear in Economics?
author: Tyler Cowen
description: Cowen argues the individual research paper is no longer scarce — AI can tweak, improve, or review any paper. Top economics journals are already experimenting with Refine for AI-powered reviewing. Suggests economists should focus on publishing "the box" rather than individual papers.
shortDescription: Cowen argues the research paper is no longer scarce — AI can review and improve any paper. Top journals already experimenting with AI reviewing.

title: Claude Code for Academics
author: Alessandro Spina
description: A gentle introduction to using Claude Code for academics. Includes presentation slides, an "Editor" persona for academic writing, and a curated collection of Claude Code tools and workflows for research.
shortDescription: Presentation slides and tools for using Claude Code in academic research, including an "Editor" persona for writing.

title: AI for Professionals Who Don't Code
author: Chris Blattman
description: Political economist Chris Blattman (UChicago Harris) documents AI tools and workflows for knowledge workers — from chatbot prompting to advanced Claude Code automation. Includes downloadable skills, templates, and case studies for managing scheduling, email, and research without coding.
shortDescription: Chris Blattman (UChicago Harris) shares AI workflows for knowledge workers — from prompting basics to Claude Code automation, with downloadable templates.

title: How Will AI-Driven Automation Actually Affect Jobs?
author: Alex Imas, Soumitra Shukla
description: Imas (UChicago Booth) and Shukla (Harvard) argue AI exposure measures are misinterpreted as displacement threats when they indicate task augmentation. The real risk lies in low-dimensional occupations where full automation creates stronger firm incentives to eliminate positions. Uses an O-Ring model to show how partial automation can complement rather than substitute human labor.
shortDescription: AI exposure measures predict augmentation, not displacement. The real risk is in low-dimensional jobs where full automation is feasible.

title: The Economic Impacts of Artificial Intelligence: A Multidisciplinary, Multi-book Review (JEL)
author: Kevin A. Bryan
description: Reviews seven books on AI's economic impact, finding strong frameworks for AI as cheap prediction and adoption barriers, but arguing the literature offers little guidance on transformative scenarios — rapid labor churn, scientific acceleration, and existential risk — that policymakers need most.
shortDescription: Bryan reviews 7 books on AI's economic impact in JEL, finding gaps in guidance on transformative AI scenarios policymakers need most.

title: Large Language Models: An Applied Econometric Framework (NBER)
author: Jens Ludwig, Sendhil Mullainathan, Ashesh Rambachan
description: Provides a rigorous econometric framework for using LLMs in empirical research. For prediction tasks, validity requires 'no training leakage.' For estimation, even high-accuracy LLM labels can bias regressions because errors correlate with covariates — the solution is a small human-coded validation sample to debias outputs. Forthcoming in Annual Review of Economics.
shortDescription: Econometric framework for LLMs in research: high accuracy alone can't protect inference — a small validation sample is needed to debias.

title: Artificial Intelligence, Competition, and Welfare (NBER)
author: Susan Athey, Fiona Scott Morton
description: Examines how market power in upstream AI affects downstream prices, industry structure, and welfare. Identifies a 'double harm' for displaced workers who face wage cuts from AI adoption and further harm from monopoly AI pricing. Derives an adoption frontier and policy implications for regulating AI usage and access fees.
shortDescription: Athey & Scott Morton analyze how AI market power creates a 'double harm' for displaced workers through adoption and monopoly pricing.

title: AI Agents for Economic Research (NBER)
author: Anton Korinek
description: Comprehensive guide to building AI agents that autonomously conduct literature reviews, write and debug code, and orchestrate entire research workflows. Includes working code examples readers can immediately use. Shows how researchers can build complete analytical tools from English descriptions, handling everything from data uploads to regression analysis to visualization.
shortDescription: Korinek's guide to building AI agents that autonomously conduct lit reviews, code, and orchestrate research workflows — with working examples.

title: 2026 ESIF Economics and AI+ML Meeting (Econometric Society)
description: Annual meeting at Cornell (June 16-17) fostering interaction between computer science and economics, with emphasis on AI/ML. Keynotes by David Blei, Annie Liang, Sendhil Mullainathan, Aaron Roth, and Stefan Wager. Co-chaired by Francesca Molinari and Éva Tardos.
shortDescription: Econometric Society meeting at Cornell (June 16-17) bridging CS and economics, with keynotes by Mullainathan, Liang, Wager, and more.

title: NBER Summer Institute 2026: Digital Economics and Artificial Intelligence
description: Three-day NBER Summer Institute session (July 22-24) on digital economics and AI, organized by Erik Brynjolfsson, Avi Goldfarb, and Catherine Tucker. Held in Cambridge, MA and streamed on YouTube. One of the premier venues for presenting frontier AI economics research.
shortDescription: Flagship NBER Summer Institute session (July 22-24) on digital economics and AI, organized by Brynjolfsson, Goldfarb, and Tucker.

title: Explainer of Ludwig, Mullainathan and Rambachan's Econometrics of LLM Paper
author: Scott Cunningham
description: Accessible walkthrough of the Ludwig/Mullainathan/Rambachan econometric framework for using LLMs in empirical research. Breaks down the key insight that LLM measurement error is non-classical and correlated with covariates, explaining why a small validation sample is essential for unbiased inference even with highly accurate LLM labels.
shortDescription: Cunningham's accessible breakdown of why LLM measurement error is non-classical and how a validation sample fixes inference.

title: Claude Code for Applied Economists (Markus Academy)
author: Paul Goldsmith-Pinkham
description: Markus Academy mini-series on using Claude Code for applied economics research (5 of 7 episodes released). Part 1: Getting Started. See also Part 2: Data Analysis, Part 3: Web Scraping, Part 4: Large Datasets and Structured Databases, and Part 5: Writing & Thinking.
shortDescription: Markus Academy mini-series on Claude Code for applied economists: Getting Started, Data Analysis, Web Scraping, Large Datasets, and Writing & Thinking.

title: Forecasting the Economic Effects of AI
author: Forecasting Research Institute
description: Large-scale forecasting exercise surveying 69 leading economists, 52 AI experts, 38 superforecasters, and 401 members of the general public on AI's economic impact. Under rapid AI progress scenarios, economists forecast labor force participation dropping from 62.6% to 55% by 2050, with the richest 10% holding 80% of national wealth. In baseline scenarios, GDP growth and labor participation remain close to today's levels. Over 200 pages of detailed forecasts and methodology.
shortDescription: Survey of 69 economists, 52 AI experts, and 38 superforecasters on AI's economic impact — from GDP growth to inequality under multiple scenarios.

title: Building Pro-Worker Artificial Intelligence (NBER)
author: Daron Acemoglu, David Autor, Simon Johnson
description: Defines pro-worker technologies as those that expand worker capabilities and make human skills more valuable. Distinguishes five categories of AI-driven technological change: labor-augmenting, capital-augmenting, automating, expertise-leveling, and new task-creating. Argues that policy and design choices can steer AI development toward complementing workers rather than replacing them. Published jointly with Brookings/Hamilton Project.
shortDescription: Acemoglu, Autor & Johnson define five categories of AI technological change and argue policy can steer AI toward complementing workers.

title: The Politics of AI (NBER)
author: Nicholas Bloom, Christos Makridis
description: Uses Gallup Workforce Panel data to examine partisan differences in workplace AI adoption. While Democrats report higher frequent AI use (30.1% vs. 25% for Republicans in Q1 2026), this gap shrinks to statistical insignificance after controlling for education and reverses sign with occupation and industry fixed effects. Suggests the partisan AI divide is driven by educational and occupational sorting, not ideology.
shortDescription: Bloom & Makridis find the partisan AI adoption gap is driven by educational and occupational sorting, not ideology — using Gallup data.

title: AI, Employment, and Education (EconTalk)
author: Tyler Cowen, Russ Roberts
description: Tyler Cowen makes the case for integrating AI into higher education and argues college classes should devote significant time to learning how to use AI. Discusses the future of writing and thinking in academia, Cowen's solution to cheating concerns, and whether there's value to education designed to help students become who they want to be rather than ensure mastery of a subject. Cowen also shares how he personally has adapted to AI in his own workflow.
shortDescription: Tyler Cowen argues for integrating AI into higher education and shares how he has adapted to AI in his own workflow.

title: Some Thoughts on AI and Research
author: Isaiah Andrews
description: Clark Medal winner Isaiah Andrews (MIT) wrote this note originally for his PhD advisees, then shared it widely. Lays out scenarios for how AI capabilities might evolve and what each means for economics research careers. Key advice: most students are under-investing in learning these tools; pay for the better models; and learn to audit AI output, since models produce plausible-looking results that can be wrong in ways requiring expertise to detect. Widely discussed after Tyler Cowen highlighted it on Marginal Revolution.
shortDescription: Clark Medal winner Isaiah Andrews (MIT) lays out AI scenarios for economics PhD students and advises on adapting research skills.

title: Codex vs. Claude Code for Economists
author: Aniket Panjwani
description: Panjwani compares OpenAI's Codex and Anthropic's Claude Code for economics research workflows, discussing the strengths and trade-offs of each tool for applied economists.
shortDescription: Comparison of Codex and Claude Code for economics research workflows, discussing strengths and trade-offs of each tool.

title: Coarse — AI Paper Reviewer
author: David van Dijcke
description: Open-source AI referee reports for academic papers. No account needed — you pay the API cost directly (typically under $2 per review, 20+ detailed comments). Blind-evaluated against refine.ink, Stanford Agentic Reviewer, and reviewer3.com; scores higher on coverage, specificity, and depth. MIT licensed. See also GitHub.
shortDescription: Open-source AI referee reports for under $2 per review. Blind-evaluated higher than refine.ink and Stanford Agentic Reviewer.

title: Rethinking Coding Assessment in an AI-Assisted World
author: Marina Visintini, Maria Jones, Ankriti Singh
description: World Bank Development Impact blog on how AI tools like Claude Code and Stata MCP now score 77–81% on technical hiring assessments — comparable to median applicants. Rather than restricting AI use, the authors propose evaluating how candidates interact with AI tools, including reviewing chat transcripts alongside final code.
shortDescription: World Bank blog: AI coding tools now match median applicants on technical hiring tests. Proposes evaluating AI interaction skills instead.

title: Feedback Machines: AI for Research Paper Review
author: Claes Bäckman
description: Two-part series on using AI to review and improve academic papers. Part 1 covers using Cursor and Claude Code for writing, editing, and getting referee-style feedback. Part 2 introduces free Claude Code skills for structured paper review, pre-analysis plan review, grant review, and code–paper correspondence checking. All tools available on GitHub.
shortDescription: Two-part series plus free Claude Code skills for paper review, grant review, pre-analysis plans, and code-paper correspondence checks.

title: Codex Plugin for Claude Code
author: OpenAI
description: Official OpenAI plugin that brings Codex into Claude Code workflows. Three commands: /codex:review for a read-only code review, /codex:adversarial-review for a steerable challenge review, and /codex:rescue to hand work off to Codex for a second pass from a different agent. Open source.
shortDescription: Official OpenAI plugin for Claude Code: normal review, adversarial review, and task handoff to Codex. Open source.

title: Feynman — Open Source AI Research Agent
author: Companion AI
description: Open-source CLI tool for AI-powered research workflows. Supports deep research briefs with citations, literature reviews, paper auditing against codebases, and experiment replication. Uses multiple research agents (Researcher, Reviewer, Writer, Verifier) with AlphaXiv integration for paper search.
shortDescription: Open-source CLI for AI-powered research: deep research briefs, literature reviews, paper audits, and experiment replication.

title: Claude Code as an Empirical Economist: Like Humans but Without the Tails (SSRN)
author: Serafin Grundl
description: A 51-page paper from the Federal Reserve Board benchmarking Claude Code as an empirical economist. The subtitle 'Like Humans but Without the Tails' suggests the AI performs comparably to human economists on average but with less variance in output quality.
shortDescription: Federal Reserve Board paper benchmarking Claude Code as an empirical economist — comparable to humans on average, with less variance.

title: Anthropic Courses
author: Anthropic
description: Anthropic's official educational repository with five hands-on courses: API Fundamentals, Prompt Engineering Interactive Tutorial, Real World Prompting, Prompt Evaluations, and Tool Use. All courses are Jupyter notebooks with practical exercises.
shortDescription: Anthropic's official courses: API fundamentals, prompt engineering, real-world prompting, evaluations, and tool use.

title: How Does AI Distribute the Pie? Large Language Models and the Ultimatum Game (NBER)
author: Douglas K.G. Araujo, Harald Uhlig
description: Investigates how various LLMs behave in the Ultimatum Game, varying stake sizes and opponent type (human vs. AI). Finds that while some models approximate the rational benchmark, a distinct 'altruistic' mode emerges where LLMs propose hyper-fair distributions (>50%). Highlights the need for careful testing before deploying AI agents in economic settings.
shortDescription: How do LLMs split the pie? Experiments in the Ultimatum Game reveal altruistic, rational, and human-mimicking modes across models.

title: We Won't Be Missed: Work and Growth in the AGI World (NBER)
author: Pascual Restrepo
description: Argues that compute — not human capability — will be the scarce resource in an AGI economy. Most jobs won't be automated because replacing them wouldn't be worth the computing cost, not because they require uniquely human skills. Forthcoming in 'The Economics of Transformative AI' (Agrawal, Brynjolfsson & Korinek, eds.).
shortDescription: In an AGI world, compute is the scarce resource — most jobs won't be automated because replacing them isn't worth the cost.

title: Scaling Reproducibility: An AI-Assisted Workflow for Large-Scale Replication and Reanalysis (arXiv)
author: Yiqing Xu, Leo Yang
description: Develops an AI-assisted workflow (using Claude Code and ChatGPT) that automates full-paper replication at scale — retrieving materials, reconstructing environments, executing code, and matching outputs to reported estimates. Applied to 384 studies (3,382 models) from top political science journals, finding reproducibility rates rose from 29.6% to 79.8% after data archiving mandates.
shortDescription: AI-assisted workflow automates large-scale paper replication across 384 studies and 3,382 models from top political science journals.

title: AI, Price Theory, and the Future of Economics Research
author: Lynne Kiesling
description: Argues that AI is a shock to relative prices inside the academic knowledge economy: as routine empirical execution gets cheaper, the value of institutional reasoning, judgment, and price theory rises. Predicts a revival of transaction cost economics and new institutional economics as AI makes it feasible to work with messier, qualitative evidence.
shortDescription: AI reshapes economics by making empirical execution cheap — elevating the value of institutional reasoning and price theory.

title: Forecasting the Economic Effects of AI (NBER)
author: Ezra Karger, Otto Kuusela, Jason Abaluck, Kevin A. Bryan, Basil Halperin, Todd R. Jones, Connacher Murphy, Philip Trammell, Josh Rosenberg, Philip Tetlock, et al.
description: Elicits forecasts from five groups — academic economists, AI company employees, policy researchers, accurate forecasters, and the general public — about AI's economic impact. Finds expectations of substantial AI capability advances by 2030, modest labor force participation declines, and 2.5% annual GDP growth. Under a rapid AI advancement scenario, forecasters project ~4% GDP growth and labor force participation falling to 55% by 2050. Expert disagreement stems primarily from differing views on highly capable AI's economic effects rather than on the pace of AI progress.
shortDescription: Elicits AI economic forecasts from five expert and public groups; disagreement centers on AI's effects, not the pace of progress.

title: AI Assistance Reduces Persistence and Hurts Independent Performance (arXiv)
author: Grace Liu, Brian Christian, Tsvetomira Dumbalska, Michiel A. Bakker, Rachit Dubey
description: Large-scale experiments show that after just ~10 minutes of AI-assisted problem-solving, participants gave up more frequently and performed worse once the AI was removed, compared to those who never used it. The persistence costs were concentrated among users who prompted AI to solve tasks directly rather than seeking hints. Effects replicated across arithmetic and reading comprehension, suggesting a general consequence of AI-assisted problem-solving rather than a domain-specific one.
shortDescription: After ~10 min of AI-assisted problem-solving, users gave up more and performed worse without AI — especially those who sought direct solutions.

title: How AI Aggregation Affects Knowledge (NBER)
author: Daron Acemoglu, Tianyi Lin, Asuman Ozdaglar, James Siderius
description: Examines how AI systems that synthesize population beliefs as training data influence social learning. Using an extended DeGroot model with an AI aggregator, introduces a 'learning gap' metric. Key finding: rapid updating degrades learning, while slower updates and localized aggregators trained on specialized information consistently improve outcomes. Consolidating local systems into a single global aggregator diminishes performance.
shortDescription: Acemoglu et al. show that AI knowledge aggregators can improve or degrade social learning depending on speed and scope of training.

title: Trade in AI-Related Products (NBER)
author: Michael E. Waugh
description: Documents international trade patterns in AI-related goods using an LLM classification tool. AI-related products account for 23% of U.S. imports in 2025, with 73% growth since 2023 vs. 3% for non-AI products. Mexico and Taiwan dominate, accounting for roughly half of all U.S. AI-related trade. The U.S. goods trade deficit would have been nearly $200 billion smaller in 2025 without the AI expansion.
shortDescription: AI-related goods now account for 23% of U.S. imports, with 73% growth since 2023. Mexico and Taiwan dominate bilateral flows.

title: Use of Gen AI in the Workplace and the Value of Access to Training
author: Ali Hashim, Gizem Kosar, Wilbert van der Klaauw
description: NY Fed research using the November 2025 Survey of Consumer Expectations. College graduates are more than twice as likely to use AI at work (58.7% vs. 22.9%). Only 15.9% of employers provide AI training despite 38% of workers viewing it as important. Workers without AI training access would accept an 11.4% salary cut to gain it; those with access require a 24.2% raise to give it up.
shortDescription: NY Fed: Workers value AI training at 11% of salary. College grads are 2x more likely to use AI at work, but only 16% of employers offer training.

title: What Will Be Scarce?
author: Alex Imas
description: Argues AI won't cause mass unemployment but will trigger structural economic transformation. Drawing on structural change economics, Girard's mimetic desire theory, and consumer expenditure data, Imas shows that income effects account for over 75% of observed structural change. As commodity production gets automated, spending and employment shift toward a 'relational sector' — nursing, education, hospitality, artisanal work — where human involvement is intrinsic to value.
shortDescription: Imas argues AI triggers structural change, not mass unemployment — spending shifts toward 'relational' sectors where human involvement is the value.

title: Claude Code in VS Code — For Academic Economists: A Practical Guide
author: Claes Bäckman
description: Practical guide to using Claude Code inside VS Code for academic economic research. Covers installation and setup, recommended extensions for Stata, Python, R, and LaTeX, file format handling, project customization via CLAUDE.md and reusable skill commands, Git integration, and context window management. Tailored to empirical economics workflows such as robustness checks, panel regressions, and research feedback automation.
shortDescription: Practical guide for academic economists on installing, configuring, and optimizing Claude Code in VS Code for R, Stata, Python, and LaTeX workflows.

title: coarse.ink — Open-Source AI Paper Reviewer
author: David Van Dijcke
description: Open-source, not-for-profit AI paper reviewer. Plug in a paper, your OpenRouter API key, and email; reviews cost under $2 using SOTA models (Claude Opus, GPT-5.4) or under $1 with open-source models. Returns an interactive panel with major and minor comments traceable to the text and tickable when addressed. Benchmarks at coarse.ink/compare (judged by Gemini-3.1-pro) rival Reviewer3, Refine.ink, and Stanford Agentic Reviewer. Reviews active for 90 days, no data retention, explicit opt-out of training on all model calls.
shortDescription: Open-source AI paper reviewer using your OpenRouter key. Costs <$2 per review, rivals Reviewer3/Refine.ink/Stanford Agentic Reviewer. No data retention.

title: Monitoring AI Adoption in the US Economy (FEDS Notes)
author: Jeffrey S. Allen
description: Federal Reserve FEDS Notes article surveying the state of AI adoption across the U.S. economy. Census data show ~18% of firms adopted AI by year-end 2025, while the Atlanta Fed's Survey of Business Uncertainty estimates 78% of the labor force works at firms that have adopted AI. Adoption is highest in professional services and finance. Newer surveys show a stronger link between adoption rates and firm size.
shortDescription: Fed survey of U.S. AI adoption: ~18% of firms adopted AI by end-2025, with highest rates in professional services and finance.

title: Why Does AI Adoption Differ So Much across Countries?
author: Alexander Bick, Adam Blandin, David Deming, Nicola Fuchs-Schündeln, Jonas Jessen
description: St. Louis Fed analysis finding that U.S. firms have a higher share of workers using AI than European firms, and that management practices are a surprisingly powerful predictor of cross-country AI adoption. A one-standard-deviation increase in the management index is associated with a 9.6 percentage point increase in AI adoption. The authors argue that narrowing the U.S.-Europe AI adoption gap may require first narrowing the management gap.
shortDescription: Management practices are a key predictor of cross-country AI adoption gaps; narrowing U.S.-Europe AI gap may require closing the management gap.
highlightDesc: St. Louis Fed evidence on why AI adoption varies across countries: US firms out-adopt European ones, and management practices are a surprisingly strong predictor — a one-SD better management index maps to +9.6pp adoption. Closing the cross-country AI gap may mean closing the management gap first.

title: Global Economic and Financial Implications of AI: Lessons from a Scenario Planning Exercise (IMF Note)
author: Karim Barhoumi, Fabia A. de Carvalho, Michael Gorbanyov, Yosuke Kido, David Koll, Dragana Ostojic, Baoping Shang, Natalia T. Tamirisa, Sally Toms, Era Dabla-Norris, Anh D. M. Nguyen, Yunhui Zhao
description: IMF staff note synthesizing insights from a high-level workshop and scenario-planning exercise co-organized with EconTAI. Argues AI should be treated as a macro-critical transition rather than a standard technology shock. Macroeconomic outcomes will depend less on frontier capability alone than on the speed and breadth of AI diffusion and institutional readiness. Covers implications for growth, labor markets, equality, financial stability, and governance.
shortDescription: IMF scenario-planning exercise: AI is a macro-critical transition; outcomes depend on diffusion speed and institutional readiness, not just capability.

title: The Household Impact of Generative AI: Evidence from Internet Browsing Behavior (arXiv)
author: Michael Blank, Gregor Schubert, Miao Ben Zhang
description: Studies generative AI's impact on U.S. households' time allocation using browsing data from 200,000+ home devices (2021–2024). Finds that ChatGPT adoption substantially increases leisure browsing while leaving productive task time unchanged — households primarily use AI for productive non-market tasks (job hunting, travel planning, shopping), freeing up leisure time. Implies large home-productivity gains from generative AI, but raises digital-divide concerns as younger, higher-income users adopt faster.
shortDescription: ChatGPT boosts home productivity 76–176% on digital chores, but freed time goes to leisure; younger/richer households adopt faster, widening digital divide.

title: Claude Academic Research
author: Mikko Rönkkö
description: A Claude Code plugin for academic research workflows. Bundles eight skills covering MCP-grounded citations, empirical integrity checks, systematic literature reviews, Zotero integration (via Better BibTeX), and parallel-critic manuscript revision. Installs from inside Claude Code via /plugin marketplace add mronkko/claude-academic-research; an interactive /setup wizard configures Zotero and metadata-source credentials. Cross-platform (Windows, macOS, Linux).
shortDescription: Claude Code plugin bundling skills for citation grounding, empirical integrity, systematic reviews, Zotero ops and parallel-critic manuscript revision.

title: Thinking with Agents: AI Tools for Teaching and Research (UVM Economics Bootcamp)
author: Erkmen G. Aslim, Emily Beam
description: Two-session bootcamp at the University of Vermont introducing economists to agentic AI tools for research and teaching. Session 1 (Apr 22) covers the difference between chat-based and agentic tools, context windows, standing instructions, voice files, and reusable skills, with live demos of website redesign and custom skill creation. Session 2 (Apr 27) focuses on research pipelines and automation — code and paper auditing, lecture-building, and web scraping workflows. Materials include downloadable PDF slide decks, a setup/prep guide, an Applications & Skills page with custom Claude Code skills (e.g., /code-review, /econ-audit), and a curated outside-resources list.
shortDescription: UVM Economics bootcamp slides on agentic AI tools for research and teaching: context windows, voice files, skills, and research pipelines.

title: Shifting Work Patterns with Generative AI (AER: Insights, forthcoming)
author: Eleanor W. Dillon, Sonia Jaffe, Nicole Immorlica, Christopher T. Stanton
description: Field experiment across 66 firms and 7,137 knowledge workers randomly given access to a generative AI assistant integrated into the email, meeting, and writing applications they already used. In the second half of the six-month experiment, the 80% of treated workers who actively used the tool spent two fewer hours per week on email and reduced their time working outside regular hours. Beyond these individual time savings the authors detect no shifts in the quantity or composition of workers' tasks, suggesting that broader reallocation of responsibilities requires institutional and team-level changes rather than just individual AI access.
shortDescription: Field experiment in 66 firms, 7,137 knowledge workers: GenAI access cut ~2 hrs/week of email but did not shift task composition absent institutional change.

title: ZeroPaper: An Autonomous Research System (SSRN)
author: Alejandro Lopez-Lira
description: Companion paper for ZeroPaper (https://github.com/alejandroll10/zeropaper), an end-to-end autonomous research pipeline that takes a domain as input and produces a paper of roughly JFQA quality with no human in the loop between launch and finish. The system is built on three premises — state and control flow live outside the model, every stage is verified rather than trusted, and termination is mechanical — and coordinates ~30 specialized agents across 10 stages and 6 adversarial gates (math audit, novelty check, mechanism review, simulated refereeing) under any of three host runtimes (Claude Code, Codex, or Gemini CLI). The paper sets out the design discipline that makes a pipeline this long terminate without drift: ten premises about LLM behavior and six derived principles. Cost is roughly $2/paper amortized under a flat-fee max subscription (~100 papers/month), versus ~1000× more on pay-per-token APIs. Released under a custom share-alike research-use license — free for non-commercial research and education, but submitting any pipeline-produced work to a journal, preprint server, conference, or thesis committee requires prior written notice, and outputs carry a non-cosmetic provenance watermark.
shortDescription: Companion paper for ZeroPaper, an autonomous research pipeline (~30 agents, 10 stages, 6 adversarial gates) producing JFQA-quality papers at ~$2 each.

title: The Intelligence Is Plenty but the Workers Are Few
author: Dan Björkegren
description: Substack essay arguing that advanced AI will play out very differently in low- and middle-income countries than in rich economies. High-income countries can absorb AI by augmenting their large stock of knowledge workers (~41% of employment), but LMICs employ far fewer skilled workers (under 10%), so grafting AI onto a thin layer of expertise yields limited gains. The piece suggests LMICs may benefit more from fully automated intelligence systems that handle complex tasks directly rather than copying wealthy-country adoption patterns — though this requires confronting infrastructure gaps, digital legibility, and institutional constraints. Frames the asymmetry as an opportunity for poorer countries to design novel economic structures around abundant intelligence.
shortDescription: Rich vs. poor countries face different AI transitions: with few skilled workers, LMICs may benefit more from fully automated intelligence than augmentation.

title: AGI Could Lower Interest Rates (SSRN)
author: Caleb Maresca
description: Develops a heterogeneous-agent asset pricing model in which transformative AI capable of automating most human labor can lower interest rates even as it dramatically accelerates growth. Under baseline calibrations, the risk-free rate falls to near zero despite growth rising from 2% to 11%, and the equity premium expands from 6% to over 20%. The key mechanism is that labor displacement risk generates massive precautionary saving demand that outweighs the higher productivity effect. Advises caution when interpreting long-term bond yields as a signal of market expectations of transformative AI. Highlighted by Tyler Cowen.
shortDescription: Heterogeneous-agent model shows AGI can lower interest rates despite 11% growth, as labor displacement risk drives precautionary saving demand.

title: When Does Automating AI Research Produce Explosive Growth? (NBER)
author: Tom Davidson, Basil Halperin, Thomas Houlden, Anton Korinek
description: Develops a semi-endogenous growth model with an innovation network to study when AI-driven automation of research leads to superexponential ('explosive') growth. Derives a condition under which two reinforcing channels — a technological feedback loop across research sectors and an economic feedback loop where higher output finances more research — overcome diminishing returns to ideas. In a simulation calibrated to AI progress trends, fully automating software research plus modest (5%) automation elsewhere produces a singularity within six years. Includes an interactive online simulator for exploring growth paths.
shortDescription: Korinek et al. model when AI automation of research triggers explosive growth; calibrated simulation yields singularity within six years.

title: Deep Research on a Loop: Using AI Agents to Construct Economic Datasets (NBER)
author: Santiago Afonso, Sebastian Galiani, Ramiro H. Gálvez, Raul A. Sosa
description: Proposes DRIL (Deep Research on a Loop), a methodology that uses AI agents to assemble datasets from publicly available sources. DRIL applies a fixed research instrument across a mapped unit space with a two-stage architecture separating design from implementation. Applied to updating the Global Tax Expenditures Database for eight Latin American and Caribbean countries, producing 129 sources and 136 evidence records at the cost of a standard LLM subscription. Argues that even partial automation of dataset construction can shift the production function of empirical economics.
shortDescription: DRIL methodology uses AI agents to automate dataset construction from public sources, demonstrated on tax expenditure data for 8 countries.

title: Understanding Firms' AI Efforts and Their Economic Impact (NBER)
author: Tania Babina
description: Reviews firm-level data on artificial intelligence and the emerging evidence on AI's economic effects. Argues that measurement is central: different AI datasets capture different objects (invention vs. use, internal capability vs. outsourcing, realized activity vs. investor perceptions) and can therefore lead to different conclusions. Develops a framework for choosing among these measures and surveys available data sources on firm AI efforts. Synthesizes evidence on AI's effects on firm growth, valuation, productivity, risk, labor, competition, and financial markets.
shortDescription: Comprehensive survey of firm-level AI data and evidence on AI's effects on growth, productivity, labor, and competition.

title: The Value of Organizational Learning Technologies (NBER)
author: Martin Beraja, Eduard Talamàs
description: Introduces a new metric called VOLT (Value of Organizational Learning Technologies) that measures the potential increase in economic output if firms could learn faster. Using 2023 U.S. Census data on business establishments, finds that VOLT for the American economy is approximately 2.0, meaning AI-driven organizational learning technologies have the potential to double aggregate economic output in the long run. Roughly three-quarters of potential gains come from extending firm lifespans rather than boosting productivity directly. Industry-by-industry analysis reveals that knowing how exposed an industry is to LLMs tells almost nothing about how much it stands to gain from AI as an organizational learning tool.
shortDescription: New VOLT metric estimates AI-driven organizational learning could double US economic output; industry analysis challenges conventional wisdom.

title: Prism: AI-Native LaTeX Workspace for Scientific Research
description: Free cloud-based LaTeX editor with AI assistant (GPT-5.2) embedded directly into the research writing workflow. Features include contextual AI assistance with access to the full project, visual-to-code conversion for diagrams, literature search and citation integration, and real-time collaboration. Particularly relevant for economists writing papers with mathematical models and empirical tables. Free for anyone with a ChatGPT account, with enterprise versions for universities forthcoming.
shortDescription: Free AI-powered LaTeX workspace for research writing, with contextual AI help, citation tools, and real-time collaboration.

title: How (Un)stable Are LLM Occupational Exposure Scores? (NBER)
author: Michelle Yin, Hoa Vu, Claudia Persico
description: Demonstrates that LLM-based occupational AI exposure measures — widely used to estimate AI's labor market effects — are highly fragile. Replicating the dominant rubric with three frontier models on all 18,797 O*NET tasks, mean exposure diverges 3.6-fold (one model rates 14% of tasks as directly exposed while another rates 51%). In difference-in-differences employment regressions, coefficient magnitudes vary 2.4-fold across annotators, and county-level estimates flip sign depending on which model is used. Formalizes this as non-classical measurement error, cautioning against treating evolving LLMs as static instruments.
shortDescription: LLM-based AI exposure measures are highly fragile: 3.6-fold divergence across models, with employment regression results flipping sign by annotator.

title: What a Panel of Economists Said About AI in the Production of Research
author: Scott Cunningham, Kosali Simon
description: Writeup of a moderated panel at the NBER Applications of AI in Healthcare meeting (May 8, 2026) featuring Cunningham, Simon, David Bradford, and Coady Wing, with commentary from Emily Beam, Jason Fletcher, and Paul Goldsmith-Pinkham. Key themes: autonomous AI papers are crossing into top-journal quality distributions but verification doesn't scale; AI-assisted specification searching leaves no audit trail; journal editors face a flood of competent-but-uninteresting submissions; restricted-data norms collide with AI tooling; and incentives — not technology — will determine whether AI makes the field better or just bigger.
shortDescription: NBER panel on AI and research production: autonomous papers reaching top-journal quality, verification gaps, and the flood facing journal editors.

title: AI and the Research O-Ring
author: Paul Goldsmith-Pinkham
description: Argues research follows an O-ring production function (Kremer 1993): output is the product of input qualities across stages, so one weak link drags the whole chain down. AI excels at code, tables, and technical error-catching but remains weaker at ideation and writing — and understanding what an AI agent did is itself costly time. Uses METR benchmarks to show that while 50% reliability is growing exponentially, 80% reliability grows from a much lower base with equivalent uncertainty. Warns against nihilism: the set of feasible research questions has expanded, and the interesting question is which problems economists choose to deploy these tools against.
shortDescription: Research follows an O-ring production function: AI excels at some inputs but human judgment still anchors the weak links.

title: The Ideation Bottleneck: Decomposing the Quality Gap Between AI-Generated and Human Economics Research (arXiv)
author: Ning Li
description: Analyzes 953 economics papers — 912 AI-generated from the APE project and 41 human papers published in the AER and AEJ: Economic Policy — to decompose the quality gap into idea quality and execution quality. The idea gap is large (human papers achieve 47.1% mean exceptional probability vs. 16.5% for AI; Cohen's d = 2.23), while the execution gap is smaller (4.38/5.0 vs. 3.84). Idea quality accounts for roughly 71% of the overall quality difference. Only 7 AI papers (0.8%) surpass the median human paper on both dimensions simultaneously, suggesting ideation remains the primary bottleneck to competitive AI-generated economics research.
shortDescription: Idea quality, not execution, is the main bottleneck: human econ papers score 47% vs. 17% exceptional probability, accounting for 71% of the quality gap.

title: Will AI kill the research paper?
author: Tyler Cowen
description: Envisions a future where static research papers are replaced by AI-powered 'meta-papers' or 'boxes' — living documents that can be updated with new data, re-run with alternative specifications, and queried by readers in real time. Imagines Fed researchers spending careers improving a monetary-policy meta-paper rather than writing individual papers. Asks whether the people who excel at building these systems will be the same people who become top economists today, and whether the endeavor will be centralized or decentralized.
shortDescription: Envisions AI-powered 'meta-papers' replacing static research: living documents updated with new data, alternative specs, and reader queries in real time.

title: AI's Macroeconomic Challenges and Promises
author: Simone Lenzu
description: NY Fed Liberty Street Economics post examining the tension between AI's long-run productivity promise and its short-run costs for inflation, real activity, and financial stability. Notes that major AI firms committed ~$300 billion in capex in 2025 across semiconductors, power grids, and specialized labor, with AI-driven demand pushing up prices. Argues the key macro question is whether AI raises productivity faster than it raises adoption costs. Documents how AI companies shifted from retained-earnings-funded investment to raising over $100 billion in new debt by late 2025, with implications for credit markets and financial stability.
shortDescription: NY Fed analysis of AI's macro tension: $300B in AI capex drives inflation pressures while long-run productivity gains remain uncertain.

title: Artificial Intelligence–Powered (Finance) Scholarship (JEL)
author: Robert Novy-Marx, Mihail Velikov
description: Published in the Journal of Economic Literature, demonstrates a pipeline for mass-producing academic finance papers using LLMs. After mining 30,000+ potential return predictors from accounting data, the authors use Claude to generate nearly 400 complete, publication-ready papers with distinct theoretical justifications — each indistinguishable from human-authored research. Serves as both a proof of concept for AI-enhanced research efficiency and a cautionary tale about industrializing HARKing (hypothesizing after results are known). Highlighted by Tyler Cowen.
shortDescription: JEL paper shows LLMs can mass-produce ~400 publication-ready finance papers in 12 hours — a proof of concept and cautionary tale about AI-driven HARKing.

title: Tyler Cowen on the Economics of AI (Sana AI Summit)
author: Tyler Cowen
description: Twenty-minute keynote at the Sana AI Summit in New York. Cowen forecasts AI will add roughly half a percentage point to economic growth — a deliberately sober estimate, because organizations and regulators cannot keep up with the technology. Argues that AI will not cause mass unemployment but will change most jobs, and that the real winners will be people who take initiative in figuring out how AI and agents work, not those with the highest raw intelligence.
shortDescription: Cowen forecasts AI adds ~0.5pp to growth; argues initiative beats intelligence and organizational frictions limit AI's macro impact.

title: An AI Guide for Economists
author: Adrien Matray
description: A practical guide for economists and pre-doc RAs on working with Claude Code, built around "mindset before tooling" — the right mental model, setup, hard rules, an FAQ on common mistakes, and the failure modes to watch for. Emphasizes treating AI as a collaborator that needs careful verification rather than relying on prompt-engineering tricks.
shortDescription: A practical Claude Code guide for economists and RAs — mental model, setup, hard rules, and verification habits over prompt tricks.

title: Empirical Work in the Age of AI (Stanford)
author: Aniket Panjwani
description: A readable, talk-by-talk transcript of Stanford's 3.5-hour "Empirical Work in the Age of AI" conference — featuring Susan Athey, Matt Gentzkow, Andrew Hall, and others — compiled so you can pass the whole thing to a coding agent and extract exactly what is useful for your own work.
shortDescription: Readable, talk-separated transcript of Stanford's 'Empirical Work in the Age of AI' conference (Athey, Gentzkow, Hall, and others).

title: OpenAI Codex Full Course: Build & Ship
author: Aniket Panjwani
description: A free ~4-hour video course on agentic coding with OpenAI Codex aimed at economists and researchers, assuming zero experience. Steps through fundamentals — Skills, MCPs, plugins, Git, subagents, and worktrees — with immediate practical payoff, 229 companion slides, and a capstone that builds a web app from scratch.
shortDescription: Free 4-hour Codex course for economists — Skills, MCPs, Git, subagents, worktrees, 229 slides, and a build-an-app capstone.

title: econtools: Claude Code Skills for Economics Research
author: Johan Fourie
description: An open-source suite of Claude Code skills for economics research. Its "/tyler" skill (named for Tyler Cowen) converts a folder of academic PDFs into a token-efficient markdown wiki — one lightweight file per paper plus an index — so Claude Code can load an entire literature into context without burning tokens on raw PDF parsing. The suite also includes simulated peer review and more.
shortDescription: Open-source Claude Code skills for economists — '/tyler' turns a folder of PDFs into a token-efficient literature wiki, plus peer review.

title: Reviewer: Multi-Agent Referee for Economics Papers
author: Ingar Haaland
description: An open-source, multi-agent reviewer for economics papers that runs locally with Codex. It turns a PDF into a structured, high-quality referee report through a modular, highly customizable pipeline in which every finding is traceable back to a specific agent.
shortDescription: Open-source multi-agent referee for economics papers — runs locally with Codex, turning a PDF into a structured, fully traceable report.

title: Academic Research Skills: A 10-Stage Claude Code Pipeline
author: Cheng-I Wu
description: A free, open-source 10-stage academic research pipeline for Claude Code. It hunts references, formats citations, writes section by section, and runs a simulated peer-review panel (including a "devil's advocate"), with integrity gates that catch fabricated citations and statistical errors. A full 15,000-word paper runs roughly $4–6 in API credits.
shortDescription: Free 10-stage Claude Code academic pipeline — deep research, drafting, simulated peer review, and integrity checks for fabricated citations.

title: Claude Code 101 for Academic Researchers
author: Mushtaq Bilal
description: A five-part, jargon-free tutorial that helps researchers with no technical background get started with Claude Code — installing it like any app, batch-processing dozens of PDFs at once, coding qualitative interview transcripts, and cleaning up messy spreadsheets.
shortDescription: Five-part, no-jargon tutorial for researchers new to Claude Code — batch-process PDFs, code interview transcripts, and clean messy data.

title: Coding Agents in the Social Sciences (Anthropic Economic Research)
author: Thomas Lyttelton, Maxim Massenkoff, Nathan Wilmers
description: Research from Anthropic's economics team on how AI agents able to execute research end-to-end will reshape social science. It tests coding agents on real social-science tasks and asks to what extent AI may automate innovation and change research productivity.
shortDescription: Anthropic Economic Research on AI agents that execute social-science research end-to-end — and how far they can automate innovation.

title: zewwwwEcon: Quarto Templates for Applied Economics
author: Simon Reif
description: Open-source Quarto templates and example project structures for reproducible applied-economics research, designed so AI coding agents work well on top of a fully scripted pipeline from raw data to publishable output (with optional Make and Nix).
shortDescription: Quarto project templates for reproducible applied-economics research, structured so AI coding agents work cleanly over a scripted pipeline.

title: Econ Journal Matchmaker and Other AI Tools for Economists
author: Ricardo Perez-Truglia
description: A collection of AI tools for economists, including the Econ Journal Matchmaker — which suggests target journals and editors from a paper's abstract or introduction with no login required — and a "Citation Hallucination Police" that checks references for fabricated citations.
shortDescription: AI tools for economists — the no-login Econ Journal Matchmaker (journal/editor suggestions) and a checker for hallucinated citations.

title: AI Coding Agents in Social Science: Methodologically Diverse, Empirically Consistent, Interpretively Vulnerable
author: Meysam Alizadeh, Fabrizio Gilardi, Mohsen Mosleh, Enkelejda Kasneci
description: A preprint testing whether AI coding agents (Claude Code and Codex) match human methodological diversity in a "many-analysts" design on an immigration and social-policy hypothesis. The agents reproduce human-like method diversity and broadly similar effect estimates, but show a vulnerability at the interpretation layer — a confirmatory prompt flipped Claude Code's verdict from 10% to 90% support without meaningfully changing the coefficients.
shortDescription: Preprint: AI agents match human method diversity and effect estimates in a many-analysts design, but their interpretations are easily biased.

title: Linking VS Code and Overleaf — For Academic Economists
author: Claes Bäckman
description: A guide for academic economists on syncing Overleaf with VS Code through either GitHub or Dropbox, so you can use Claude Code and Codex on your LaTeX projects while keeping Overleaf's collaborative editing. Recommends GitHub Desktop for versioned work and Dropbox for real-time coauthoring.
shortDescription: Guide to syncing Overleaf with VS Code (via GitHub or Dropbox) to use Claude Code and Codex on LaTeX while keeping Overleaf collaboration.

title: 10 Things on AI and Development
author: Oliver Hanney
description: A curated roundup from VoxDev's managing editor of ten of the most interesting recent pieces on AI and development, spanning research and practitioner perspectives — compiled as a counterweight to a development community he argues has been slow to engage with AI's most important questions.
shortDescription: VoxDev editor's curated roundup of ten standout recent reads on AI and economic development, from researchers and practitioners.

title: Claude Code, Economics Research, and the Returns to Expertise (The AI Economist)
author: Scott Cunningham, Aniket Panjwani
description: A one-hour interview in which Scott Cunningham joins Aniket Panjwani to discuss what agentic AI changes for empirical economics: faster research production but slower verification, difference-in-differences workflows, cross-language replication and package audits, encoding repeated checks into skills, and why domain expertise still matters when agents can produce polished output. Includes a sectioned companion transcript (some sections require a free newsletter subscription).
shortDescription: Hour-long interview with Scott Cunningham on what agentic AI changes for empirical economics — production vs. verification, and the returns to expertise.

title: What Investment Data Implies about the AI Transition (NBER)
author: Jessica Wachter, Jonathan Wachter
description: The five largest U.S. tech firms spent $380 billion on capex in 2025 and are forecast to roughly double that in 2026 — risking bankruptcy unless expected profits grow commensurately. Embeds this observation in a two-sector open-economy model with rare productivity booms. Calibrating to observed investment implies a boom raises AI-sector productivity by a factor of 2.7, with additional cumulative GDP growth of 5–58 percentage points by 2030 and AI shares of the economy ranging from 8% to 39%.
shortDescription: Big Tech's $380B AI capex implies a 2.7x productivity boom; model projects 5–58pp additional GDP growth by 2030 across scenarios.

title: Can AI Refute Economic Theory? Evidence from Beyond the Knowledge Cutoff (arXiv)
author: Alexis Akira Toda
description: Tests whether AI models (Gemini, Refine, Claude, ChatGPT) can find errors in four published economic theory papers, each containing a known mistake. ChatGPT Pro performed best, occasionally constructing counterexamples and corrected proofs, while other models fared worse. No model located a true error without substantial human guidance. Argues a competent human paired with a frontier model can outperform current peer review, but AI cannot yet refute economic theory on its own. Highlighted by Tyler Cowen on Marginal Revolution.
shortDescription: Tests AI models on finding errors in published economic theory — none succeeded without guidance, but human+AI can outperform peer review.

title: AI Economic Indicators (Stanford Digital Economy Lab)
author: Connacher Murphy, Erik Brynjolfsson
description: New freely accessible platform from the Stanford Digital Economy Lab to track how AI is reshaping work, productivity, and value creation. The first release introduces three related efforts: the Canaries Dashboard (tracking employment trends by AI exposure level, built with ADP Research), the Takeoff Tracker (evaluating evidence for AI-driven explosive growth), and regularly updated research notes. Aims to replace anecdotes and lagging indicators with timely, trusted evidence.
shortDescription: Stanford's new free platform tracking AI's economic impact — employment canaries, a growth takeoff tracker, and research notes.

title: revise-applied-paper: A Claude Code Skill for Refereeing Applied Economics Papers
author: Noé J Nava
description: An open-source Claude Code skill that acts as an automated journal referee for applied economics manuscripts (.qmd, .md, or .tex). It runs a cold subagent that audits the draft against an ~80-item checklist distilled from Marc F. Bellemare's Doing Economics (MIT Press, 2022), produces a referee report with numbered major and minor comments, then applies editing-level fixes while parking substantive items in a to-do ledger. Runs locally and free on top of Claude, supports interactive and autonomous loop modes, and anchors every comment to a citable authority rather than a model's taste. A writing-craft tool, not scientific peer review.
shortDescription: Open-source Claude Code skill that referees applied econ papers against Bellemare's Doing Economics — runs locally, free, anchored to a citable authority.

title: How AI Reshapes Skill Demand in European Firms (LISER Policy Brief)
author: Terry Gregory, Najada Feimi, Christina Gathmann, David Marguerit
description: LISER policy brief drawing on more than 75 million online job vacancies from Belgium, France, Germany, and Luxembourg between 2018 and 2023 to track how employers' skill requirements evolve as occupations become more exposed to AI. It argues AI is reshaping the content of jobs rather than eliminating them: demand is rising fast for AI-related analytical skills, employers increasingly seek workers who combine analytical tools with judgment and leadership, and the adjustment happens largely within existing occupations. Concludes the policy priority should be reskilling and upskilling within current occupational trajectories.
shortDescription: LISER brief using 75M+ EU job vacancies (2018–2023): AI rewires skill demand within occupations rather than replacing jobs.

title: AI in Economics: A Weekly Research Roundup
author: Kosali Simon
description: A weekly Substack newsletter from the O'Neill School of Public and Environmental Affairs at Indiana University that scans new working-paper listings (the NBER 'New This Week' email, the NEP-AIN digest from RePEc, and Google Scholar alerts) and summarizes the most notable new economics research on AI. It covers three angles: AI as a subject of economic study (labor, productivity, trade, public finance), AI as a tool for doing economics (LLMs, ML, agentic coding), and AI as an economic actor (agents that bargain, trade, and compete). Each post offers a paragraph or two per paper with hyperlinked titles; the launch edition includes a full Q1 2026 catch-up archive.
shortDescription: Weekly Substack roundup of new AI-in-economics working papers, curated by Kosali Simon (Indiana University) across labor, methods, and AI agents.

title: research-craft: An Agent Skill for Better Research Loops
author: Nikita Nosov
description: An open-source agent skill in the SKILL.md format, installable into Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI and other agents via the skills CLI, that turns vague research work into a tight loop: choosing better problems, improving inputs, forecasting before experiments, keeping research logs, inspecting failures, and publishing useful artifacts. Based on Vivek's essay 'how to be good at research.' Oriented toward ML/AI experiment design rather than economics specifically, but useful for structuring any empirical research workflow.
shortDescription: Open-source agent skill (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor...) for tighter research loops: pick problems, forecast experiments, log, inspect failures.

title: From Microeconomics to AI Research: A Guide for Economists (SSRN)
author: Pavel Kireyev, Roberto Rafael Maura Rivero
description: A 26-page guide arguing that the decisions shaping how AI systems are built and aligned are largely microeconomic problems. It opens with a self-contained primer on the RLHF pipeline, showing that reward modeling, preference aggregation, and policy optimization rest on equivalences with discrete choice, social choice, and principal-agent models. It then maps specific competencies (behavioral economics for annotator biases, mechanism design for feedback elicitation, social choice for preference aggregation, contract theory and information design for alignment, game theory for multi-agent safety, production economics for compute scaling laws) to concrete AI research problems, and closes with practical paths into academia and AI labs plus a companion repository.
shortDescription: Guide mapping micro fields (mechanism design, social choice, contract theory) to LLM post-training and alignment, with a path into AI research.

title: Agentic coding and persistent returns to expertise (Anthropic)
author: Zoe Hitzig, Maxim Massenkoff, Eva Lyubich, Shaoyi Zhang, Ryan Heller, Peter McCrory
description: Anthropic Economic Research report based on a privacy-preserving analysis of ~400,000 Claude Code sessions from ~235,000 people (October 2025 to April 2026). It introduces a framework describing what work is done, who does it, and whether it succeeds. Key findings: people make ~70% of planning decisions while Claude makes ~80% of execution decisions; domain expertise (not coding proficiency) drives success, with sessions rated expert reaching verified success more than twice as often as novice ones; non-software occupations succeed within seven points of software engineers; and the estimated value of the typical task rose ~25% over the seven months.
shortDescription: Anthropic study of ~400k Claude Code sessions: domain expertise, not coding skill, drives success; non-coders succeed near software engineers.

title: Why Your Codex Goals Suck
author: Aniket Panjwani
description: Short video on how economists can get more out of hours-long Codex and Claude Code 'goals' for research. Panjwani demonstrates converting Kirill Borusyak, Xavier Jaravel, and Jann Spiess's Stata/Python difference-in-differences imputation package into an R package via a ~15-hour overnight Codex goal, emphasizing the importance of defining validation criteria up front rather than leaving them to the agent, and showing how to use Codex and Claude Code together.
shortDescription: Video demoing a ~15-hour Codex goal to port a Stata/Python DiD package to R, with tips on defining validation criteria up front.

title: CoPaper.AI
author: Stanford REAP / StatsPAI
description: An AI research co-authoring platform from Stanford's REAP program (founder Bryce Wang; co-founder and strategic advisor Scott Rozelle). Users upload data (CSV, Excel, JSON, Parquet; up to 20 datasets), set a research direction, and the system generates an empirical paper chapter by chapter with human-in-the-loop review, exporting a complete DOCX with full, reproducible code in Stata, R, and EViews. It supports methods from OLS, logit/probit, fixed effects, and IV to DiD, RDD, synthetic control, decomposition, and causal forests. As a new platform, its track record is still limited.
shortDescription: Stanford REAP's AI co-authoring platform: upload data, generate an empirical econ paper chapter by chapter with reproducible Stata/R/EViews code.

title: Writing Code vs. Shipping Code: Productivity Effects Across Generations of AI Coding Tools (SSRN)
author: Mert Demirer, Leon Musolff, Liyuan Yang
description: A matched event-study using data on 100,000+ GitHub developers and their AI-usage telemetry to estimate the productivity effects of successive AI coding tools. Autocomplete, interactive coding agents, and autonomous agents raise commits by 40%, 140%, and 180% respectively, but these gains attenuate up the production chain: the 180% commit effect falls to 50% for projects and just 30% for actual releases. The authors interpret this through a weak-link model with an estimated 0.25 elasticity of substitution between AI and human effort (strong complementarity), and confirm the pattern across four app marketplaces. A MIT Sloan working paper.
shortDescription: MIT Sloan event-study of 100k+ GitHub devs: AI coding agents lift commits 180% but only 30% of that reaches actual releases—human bottlenecks bind.

title: Theorist Toolbox: Tools for Agent-Based LLM-Assisted Economic Theory Research (arXiv)
author: Moran Koren
description: Argues that by 2026 the binding constraint on machine-assisted economic theory is no longer producing mathematics but trusting it, since a fluent model will prove a false theorem as readily as a true one. Proposes a verification-first protocol instantiated as three methods that differ in how work is checked: a single disciplined pass, an adversarial prover-verifier pair (Claude Opus 4.8 proposing, OpenAI Codex refuting, the author triaging), and a structured multi-agent project with a reviewer gate. Demonstrated on a worked mechanism-design example (a Groves/Pigouvian incentive mechanism for the Gans-Kominers grade-inflation model), concluding that external verification, not model capability, is the key design variable.
shortDescription: A verification-first protocol for LLM-assisted economic theory, using an adversarial prover-verifier loop—external checking, not model capability, is key.

title: Using Claude Code for academic work
author: Pedro H. C. Sant'Anna
description: A comprehensive framework for doing academic research with Claude Code, spanning the full lifecycle from papers and data analysis to presentations. It uses 18 specialized agents and an orchestrator pattern that plans, implements, reviews, and verifies work through structured quality gates, with human oversight at each stage. Highlights include a Beamer-to-Quarto conversion pipeline, adversarial review loops, simulated peer review calibrated to major economics journals, and 52+ slash commands automating tasks such as literature review and manuscript evaluation. Reported as adopted across 15+ research groups in economics, energy, political science, and engineering.
shortDescription: An end-to-end Claude Code workflow for academic research: 18 specialized agents, an orchestrator pattern, simulated peer review, and 52+ slash commands.
highlightDesc: Pedro Sant'Anna's end-to-end Claude Code workflow for academic research: 18 specialized agents and an orchestrator that plans, implements, reviews, and verifies, plus a Beamer-to-Quarto pipeline, simulated economics-journal peer review, and 52+ slash commands.

title: AI Economist Agent: An Agentic Framework for Model-Grounded Economic Analysis (arXiv)
author: Masahiro Kato
description: Proposes a RAG-based "AI economist agent" that grounds LLM-generated economic narratives in economic theory and real-world data. Rather than producing quantitative claims with the language model alone, agents plan the analysis, retrieve evidence from knowledge graphs, select appropriate models, and generate reports linked to explicit model-based computations. Demonstrated on two applications: economist report generation for U.S. inflation persistence and Federal Reserve policy, and bank stress-test narratives for U.S. commercial real estate refinancing stress.
shortDescription: A RAG-based AI economist agent that grounds LLM narratives in economic theory and data, shown on U.S. inflation/Fed policy and bank stress-test reports.

title: ChatDiD
author: Clément de Chaisemartin
description: A custom GPT offering expert guidance on difference-in-differences (DiD), including the de Chaisemartin–D'Haultfoeuille heterogeneity-robust estimators and their Stata/R packages (e.g., did_multiplegt). It helps researchers choose the right DiD estimator for their design and accompanies the authors' forthcoming textbook, Causal Inference with Differences-in-Differences: Credible Answers to Hard Questions (Princeton University Press).
shortDescription: A custom GPT by Clément de Chaisemartin for difference-in-differences—pick the right estimator and use the de Chaisemartin–D'Haultfoeuille packages.

title: Scholara
description: An AI platform (by Stematic Labs) that automates the systematic-review and meta-analysis workflow end to end: building PICO/MeSH search strategies across PubMed, Cochrane, and other databases; triple-agent consensus abstract screening with recorded rationales; schema-based data extraction from PDFs linked back to source paragraphs; and publication-ready forest plots. It is PRISMA-2020 oriented and generates audit-ready flow diagrams, aimed at evidence-synthesis teams across the social and health sciences.
shortDescription: AI systematic-review tool: PICO/MeSH search building, triple-agent abstract screening, PDF data extraction, forest plots, PRISMA-ready audit trails.

title: academic-humanizer: Strip AI-Writing Tells from Papers and Grant Proposals
description: An open-source skill for Claude Code, Codex, and similar agents that edits AI-polished academic prose to remove tell-tale AI patterns ("In recent years…", "paves the way", rule-of-three, over-long sentences, em-dashes) while preserving scholarly voice, hedging, definitions, citations, and every number. It matches claims to evidence (no verb stronger than the data) and has a dedicated grant-proposal mode tuned to NSF/NIH structure and first-page primacy. The rules were derived by comparing AI drafts against the team's accepted papers and funded proposals.
shortDescription: A Claude Code/Codex skill that removes AI-writing tells from papers and NSF/NIH proposals while keeping scholarly voice, citations, and numbers intact.

title: A Practitioner's Guide to Using Large Language Models and Generative AI in Economic History (NBER)
author: Andreas Ferrara
description: A hands-on guide for researchers new to LLMs, setting out a step-by-step workflow for turning a research idea into working code and data. It describes the four main ways of interacting with an LLM (chat window, editor-integrated assistants, agentic coding tools, and the API) and works through practitioner decisions in sequence: whether an LLM is the right tool, whether data may be sent to one, how to select models, write prompts, manage context limits, and control costs, and finally how to validate, reproduce, document, and correct LLM-generated measures in regression settings. Includes worked examples with replication files, such as classifying emotions in paintings and linking historical census records.
shortDescription: Andreas Ferrara's step-by-step workflow for using LLMs in research: model selection, prompting, cost control, and validating LLM-generated measures.

title: The Economic Benefits and Costs of AI and Policies to Mitigate AI's Impact on Inequality (arXiv)
author: Matthew O. Jackson, Zafer Kanik
description: Models how increasingly productive AI reshapes labor reallocation and wages across worker categories: those essential to AI development see faster wage growth, workers displaced by AI experience falling wages in absolute and relative terms, and workers in final-goods production track overall output. Contrasting competitive versus monopolistic AI production (monopoly restricts deployment and slows the transition), it derives optimal tax and regulatory policies that achieve Pareto improvements and shows these differ depending on whether AI production is competitive.
shortDescription: How productive AI reshapes wages and inequality, and which tax/regulatory policies yield Pareto improvements under competitive vs. monopolistic AI.

title: Integration and Collaboration in AI Research Work
author: Paul Goldsmith-Pinkham
description: The capstone (Video 8) of Paul Goldsmith-Pinkham's Markus Academy series on Claude Code. It demonstrates a practical verification workflow for AI-generated research using git, GitHub, and issue tracking, worked through an IPO event study. The central argument: AI has slashed the cost of producing work, but verification remains expensive, creating "verification debt" that researchers must manage systematically through structured review processes borrowed from software engineering.
shortDescription: Capstone of Goldsmith-Pinkham's Claude Code series: a git/GitHub workflow for verifying AI-generated research and managing "verification debt."

title: AI Research Feedback: Claude Code Skills for Peer Review
author: Claes Bäckman
description: A collection of open-source Claude Code skills for academic research review, developed by economist Claes Bäckman. Includes a full 8-agent referee-style paper review (review-paper), a fast 2-agent check (review-paper-light), a paper-code reproducibility and alignment audit (review-paper-code), a pre-analysis plan review (review-pap), and a grant proposal review (review-grant). Installed as slash commands in Claude Code (e.g. /review-paper). A July 2026 update added strict scope discipline so agents only read the paper's source files, and replaced hallucinated novelty judgments with an adversarial advocate-vs-skeptic method.
shortDescription: Open-source Claude Code skills for academic peer review: 8-agent paper review, reproducibility audits, pre-analysis plan and grant proposal reviews.

title: The Microeconomics of Artificial Intelligence
author: Joshua Gans
description: An open-access MIT Press monograph treating AI as statistical prediction that enhances (and sometimes enables) decision-making, analysed with microeconomic tools. Gans focuses on impacts within firms and industries rather than economy-wide employment and productivity: the supply and production characteristics of AI, the drivers of demand for prediction, how supply and demand set a price for predictions and how market structure shapes that price, and the key policy trade-offs for antitrust, privacy, and other regulation. The full text is free under a CC BY-NC-ND licence.
shortDescription: Joshua Gans's open-access MIT Press book analysing AI as prediction through microeconomics — demand, supply, pricing, market structure, and policy.
