title: AI and development economics: Early evidence and how to keep up
author: Oliver Hanney
description: A continually updated VoxDev resource bank (last refreshed 8 July 2026) compiling the best sources on AI and development economics: early evidence on AI's impacts in low- and middle-income countries, what development organisations are working on, how development economists can use AI in their research, and how to keep up. Argues the field risks failing on AI's most important questions and points to early examples of the work needed.
shortDescription: VoxDev editor Oliver Hanney's living bank of the best sources on AI and development economics — evidence, tools, and how to keep up.

title: Where the Returns to AI Go
author: Brian Albrecht
description: An Economic Forces essay applying price theory to the AI boom: distinguishing creating value from capturing it, and arguing that even if AI generates enormous value, the returns need not flow to the big model labs — they accrue to whoever owns the genuinely scarce, complementary resources. A corrective to both AI 'boomer' and 'doomer' assumptions about where the money goes.
shortDescription: Price-theory take on who actually captures AI's economic returns — model labs, workers, or owners of scarce complementary inputs.

title: "We Must Act Now": Sixteen Nobel Laureates Join Leading Economists and AI Researchers in Call to Prepare for AI's Economic Transformation
description: A Stanford Digital Economy Lab announcement of an open statement signed by 16 Nobel laureates and more than 200 economists and AI researchers. It warns that AI could drive an economic transformation on the scale of the Industrial Revolution but far faster, and urges policymakers, economists, and technology leaders to prepare institutions and policies now so the gains are shared broadly rather than concentrated among a few.
shortDescription: Statement by 16 Nobel laureates and 200+ economists and AI researchers urging urgent action so AI's economic transformation benefits society broadly.

title: AI in Economics Research: From Frontier Ideas to a Working Agentic Pipeline (wiiw seminar)
author: Luka Šikić
description: Materials from a Vienna Institute for International Economic Studies (wiiw) seminar on running AI agents in empirical economics while preserving scientific integrity. Includes reveal.js slides, a PDF, a one-page handout, and a fully cloneable repository that reproduces an event-study estimation pipeline (R, Quarto, targets) on live Eurostat data, with a "plan gate" where economists approve agent proposals and a "provenance gate" ensuring every reported number traces to computed output.
shortDescription: wiiw seminar with slides, handout, and a cloneable repo reproducing an agentic event-study pipeline (R/Quarto/targets) with plan and provenance gates.

title: empirical_agent: Sandboxing and Scoring Agentic LLMs on Econometric Replication
author: Simon Firestone
description: An open-source, end-to-end framework for running, sandboxing, and scoring agentic LLMs on complex data-science and econometric replication tasks. It pairs a claude-empirical-harness that executes agents in isolated Docker environments across repeated trials with econbench_framework, a YAML-configurable scoring system that grades agent outputs against econometric benchmarks (including a pre-built Wallace housing-investment benchmark) using both automated validation and LLM-based scoring. Firestone reports replicating two graduate-level economics papers five times each, concluding that Claude and Codex agents are "at least as good as an Economics Ph.D. student who has finished their first semester."
shortDescription: Open framework to sandbox and score agentic LLMs (Claude, Codex) on econometric replication tasks, with Docker isolation and benchmark grading.

title: Grand-to-Ground (G2G): An Adversarial Research Loop for AI-Assisted Social Science
author: Hongtao Ma
description: An open-source Claude plugin (v0.1.0, MIT-licensed) that orchestrates an eight-phase, Lakatos-inspired research cycle for AI-assisted social science, aimed first at economics and finance. It turns broad theoretical frameworks into falsifiable questions using a deducer agent plus three independent critic agents (logic, evidence, novelty), a tribunal for adversarial review, automated falsifiability scoring, and plain-Markdown programme state, with human researchers as final arbiters.
shortDescription: Open-source Claude plugin running an 8-phase, Lakatos-inspired adversarial research loop with critic agents for economics and finance research.

title: AI Premium (NBER)
author: Nicola Borri, Aleh Tsyvinski, Yukun Liu
description: Using 380 trillion tokens of realized AI consumption from over 400 large language models (OpenRouter data, ~2% of global monthly token use), the authors construct an AI Factor and estimate firm-level AI Betas. High-AI-beta firms earn higher subsequent returns, with a value-weighted strategy earning 64.1 basis points weekly; the premium concentrates in intensive, frontier-oriented AI use, is absent in emerging markets, and interaction-and-communication occupations show higher market-implied AI exposure than analytical roles. The paper offers early evidence of an emerging agentic economy.
shortDescription: NBER paper mining 380 trillion AI tokens across 400+ LLMs to build an AI Factor and document a large, tradable AI Premium in stock returns.

title: Measuring AI Innovation with Trademark Data (arXiv)
author: C. Castaldi, F. Castellacci, A. Fronzetti Colladon, L. Segneri, F. Venturini
description: This research note argues that trademark data can complement patents for mapping the development and diffusion of AI. AI trademarks reveal how firms exploit AI to develop new goods and services, and offer a timely, globally available source that spans all economic sectors; the authors illustrate the approach with an empirical exploration of Italian firms and discuss how AI trademarks can be used at different levels of analysis to study AI's spread.
shortDescription: Research note proposing AI trademark data as a timely, cross-sector complement to patents for measuring the development and diffusion of AI.

title: pAI-Econ-claude: A Gated Human-in-the-Loop Multi-Agent Architecture for AI-Assisted Economic Theory Development (arXiv)
author: Chen Zhu, Xiaolu Wang, Weilong Zhang
description: Proposes a system in which Claude-based agents coordinate through a shared workspace of inspectable intermediate records, with diagnostic gates and human checkpoints, for economic theory development where no cheap, machine-readable correctness signal exists. Across five economic tasks the gated architecture improved mean failure severity from 1.58 to 1.16 and usefulness from 2.60 to 3.10; in one case it rejected a false market-structure premise that the agents would otherwise have perpetuated, preserving human authority over consequential decisions.
shortDescription: Claude-based multi-agent architecture with diagnostic gates and human checkpoints for AI-assisted economic theory development.

title: The Evolution of Digital Search: From Blue Links to Delegated Decision-Making (arXiv)
author: David M. Rothschild, Nicole Immorlica, Brendan Lucier, Markus Mobius, Aleksandrs Slivkins
description: Argues digital search is shifting from human keyword queries toward AI agents that interpret natural-language goals and return recommendations or execute decisions. The authors contend that outcomes will depend less on algorithmic refinements than on system design—information access, option presentation, transparency, and fair competition—and show how relatively modest design choices shape market efficiency, consumer welfare, and competitive dynamics in agent-driven marketplaces.
shortDescription: How AI agents are reshaping digital search into delegated decision-making, and why system design shapes competition and consumer welfare.

title: Generative AI Availability, Grades, and Student Satisfaction at a Large University (arXiv)
author: James M. Zumel Dumlao, Meng Wang, Zhonghan Xie, Junyao Hu, Ivan Bar, George Chaney III, Henry Gold, Misha Teplitskiy
description: Using 2015–2025 administrative data from a large U.S. university, the authors classify courses by their susceptibility to AI use and estimate the effect of generative-AI availability on outcomes. They find no significant differential effect of GenAI availability on grades overall or among previously lower-performing students, and similarly muted effects on self-reported understanding — evidence against fears of AI-driven grade inflation.
shortDescription: Empirical study finds no differential effect of generative-AI availability on grades or self-reported understanding at a large U.S. university.

title: Randomness in Large Language Models: What Researchers Need to Know (and Report) (arXiv)
author: Guillaume Coqueret, Joan Llull, Florian Oswald, Christophe Pérignon, Christoph Scheuch, Lars Vilhuber
description: LLM outputs vary across repeated requests even with unchanged prompts and settings — because of deliberate sampling, silent model updates, numerical rounding, and expert routing — and setting temperature to zero removes only the intentional sampling. Using sentiment analysis of corporate filings as an illustration, the authors argue LLM outputs should be treated as draws from a distribution rather than fixed measurements, and propose concrete reporting standards for researchers, authors, and data editors.
shortDescription: Why LLM outputs vary even at temperature zero, and reporting standards for researchers, authors and data editors who use them.

title: reviewer3
author: Robert Haase
description: An open-source command-line tool that uses LLMs to give constructive feedback on scientific manuscripts in .docx format. By default it runs a locally installed, privacy-preserving model via Ollama (gpt-oss:20b at localhost), and returns inline tracked edits, clarification comments, and a review preface summarizing the document, its scientific importance, and global feedback — useful for a quick referee-style pass when co-authors are unavailable.
shortDescription: Open-source CLI that reviews .docx manuscripts with a local, privacy-preserving LLM (via Ollama), returning tracked edits, comments and a review preface.

title: Using Machine Learning to Generate, Clarify, and Improve Economic Models (JEL)
author: Annie Liang
description: Forthcoming in the Journal of Economic Literature, this article examines how machine learning and other computational techniques can contribute to building economic models — clarifying a model's strengths and limitations, identifying prediction failures through adversarial testing, creating hybrid models that combine economic theory with flexible algorithms, and exploring applications of large language models in economics.
shortDescription: JEL article on how ML can help generate, stress-test, and improve economic models, including hybrid theory-plus-algorithm approaches and LLM uses.

title: Prose is not constraints and other things I learned from Paul Goldsmith-Pinkham's NBER talk on AI in empirical research
author: Scott Cunningham
description: Reflecting on Paul Goldsmith-Pinkham's NBER talk and his own large-scale experiments with semi-autonomous agents, Cunningham argues that written rules in CLAUDE.md files and prompts do not actually constrain coding agents — 'prose is not a constraint.' Real constraints come from tools (for example, an R package that refuses invalid specifications) and hooks that make forbidden actions impossible, not from instructions the agent can ignore.
shortDescription: Cunningham argues prose rules don't constrain coding agents in empirical research; only tools and hooks that forbid actions do.

title: How Economics Absorbed AI
author: Luka Šikić
description: A data-driven field map of how AI has been integrated into economics, built from 661 resources (530 with full text) across six registers — working papers, tools, commentary, guides, podcasts, and courses. It traces the field's development from 2023 to 2026, documents how different formats cite one another (papers link mostly to papers, tools to tools), and forecasts developments through 2028, arguing that 'intelligence became cheap and trust did not,' so verified judgment is the new scarce factor.
shortDescription: Field map of 661 resources on how AI entered economics, tracing citation flows across formats and forecasting the field through 2028.

title: Training AI for When Humans Will Use It (NBER)
author: Kevin A. Bryan, Joshua S. Gans
description: AI predicts, and humans use those predictions — combined with human verification, other statistical models, and further analysis — to make decisions. The authors show that maximizing an AI model's prediction accuracy alone is generally suboptimal once you account for how humans actually use it, and analyze optimal model training (using geometric methods) with heterogeneous users and a monopoly trainer.
shortDescription: NBER paper: because humans use AI predictions within larger decisions, maximizing prediction accuracy alone is suboptimal for training.

title: Project APE: Autonomous Policy Evaluation
author: Social Catalyst Lab (University of Zurich)
description: An experiment by the Social Catalyst Lab at the University of Zurich testing whether AI can autonomously generate, replicate, and revise empirical economic research from publicly available data. Generated papers are scored in an automated tournament against human-authored benchmarks from leading economics journals; as of July 2026 the project had produced over 1,000 papers and run thousands of head-to-head comparisons.
shortDescription: University of Zurich experiment testing whether AI can autonomously produce empirical policy papers, benchmarked against journal work.

title: AI Financial Advice: Supply, Demand, and Life Cycle Implications (arXiv)
author: Taha Choukhmane, Tim de Silva, Weidong Lin, Matthew Akuzawa
description: Has a representative sample write prompts asking LLMs (GPT-5.2) for spending and investing guidance, then models the life-cycle consequences of following it. Advice would move people closer to life-cycle theory (diversified equity, age-declining equity shares, larger buffers), and equity-share recommendations vary by gender, AI familiarity, and financial literacy — with a two-thirds demand-side vs one-third supply-side decomposition of the gender gap.
shortDescription: Modeling the life-cycle effects of following LLM (GPT-5.2) financial advice, and how it varies by gender, AI familiarity, and financial literacy.

title: Do Humans Bargain Differently with AI? Evidence from Alternating-Offer Games (arXiv)
author: Yuhao Fu, Nobuyuki Hanaki, Haitao Wang
description: A laboratory study using a three-stage alternating-offer bargaining game to compare how people negotiate with AI agents versus other humans. Fairness and reciprocity toward AI are weaker and more conditional than toward humans, but partially resurface when the AI’s outcomes affect real people’s payments.
shortDescription: Lab bargaining games showing fairness and reciprocity toward AI are weaker and more conditional than toward humans.

title: Talking to Digital Twins: Selective Disclosure and Belief Measurement in Financial Social Media (arXiv)
author: Boone Bowles, Raymond Duch, Sorin Sorescu
description: Uses LLMs to build and interview "digital twins" of financial influencers reconstructed from their X accounts, extracting measurable stock beliefs in real time. The resulting belief panel predicts large-cap stock returns while avoiding look-ahead bias, illustrating an LLM-based measurement approach for financial economics.
shortDescription: An LLM method that interviews "digital twins" of financial influencers to measure stock beliefs that predict large-cap returns.

title: Google's AI & Economy ATLAS v1.0: Mapping Gemini Usage in the Economy (arXiv)
author: Zanna Iscenko, Scott Strand, Yiyuan Chen, Guillaume Aimard, Mihai Codreanu, Vivek Sampathkumar, Alex Imas, Julian Jacobs, Evalyne Muiruri, Juan Mateos-Garcia, Jia Jen Ng, Samirah Javed, Josh Martin, Omar Ajmeri, Denis Calin, Andrew Kim, Fabien Curto Millet, James Manyika
description: Google's counterpart to usage-based AI economic indices: analyzes 15 million de-identified Gemini interactions mapped to over 800 occupations, 4000 tasks, 300 household activities, 150 countries, and 140 languages. Finds adoption spans roughly 88% of US employment but stays shallow and collaborative rather than fully automating tasks, covers about 98% of non-sleep US activities, and correlates with national wealth globally.
shortDescription: Maps 15M Gemini interactions across 800+ occupations, 4000 tasks, and 150 countries to chart real-world AI adoption in the economy.

title: Does Generative AI Narrow Education-Based Productivity Gaps? Evidence from a Randomized Experiment (arXiv)
author: Guillermo Cruces, Diego Fernandez Meijide, Sebastian Galiani, Ramiro Galvez, Maria Lombardi
description: A randomized online experiment with 1,174 adults aged 25-45 who completed a workplace-style problem-solving task with or without a generative AI assistant, followed by an unassisted module. AI raises performance for everyone, but gains are larger among the less educated, cutting the education-based performance gap by roughly three-quarters while assisted — though the gap partly re-emerges once the AI is removed.
shortDescription: Randomized experiment: generative AI helps everyone but helps less-educated workers most, shrinking education-based productivity gaps by ~75% while assisted.

title: World Development Report 2026: The Promise of Artificial Intelligence
author: World Bank
description: The World Bank Group’s flagship 2026 World Development Report, released 4 August 2026, is the first comprehensive assessment of AI’s implications for developing economies. It proposes an “adopt, adapt, and advance” framework and finds jobs in high-income countries are more than three times as likely to be at risk of automation by generative AI (14.2%) as in low- and middle-income countries (4.5%), while 16.2% of jobs in developing economies could see meaningful AI productivity gains.
shortDescription: World Bank flagship WDR 2026 on AI in developing economies: an “adopt, adapt, advance” framework plus evidence on uneven automation and productivity gains.

title: Better, Not More: A Research Skill Library
description: A collection of 18 markdown skill files you can drop into AI coding agents (Claude, Codex, Cursor) to raise the quality — not just the quantity — of experimental research. Assembled at the AI Workshop of the Conference on Field Experiments in Strategy at Duke, with skills contributed by scholars including Bo Cowgill, Rem Koning, and David McKenzie, covering pre-flight design audits, literature mapping, hypothesis screening, power calculations, and manuscript preparation.
shortDescription: 18 drop-in AI-agent skill files (Claude/Codex/Cursor) for better — not just more — experimental research: design audits, power calcs, and lit mapping.

title: What is really happening to jobs? Separating AI hype from reality (SIEPR)
author: Neale Mahoney, Erika McEntarfer, Karsen Wahal
description: A Stanford SIEPR policy brief synthesizing early evidence on AI and the labor market into five conclusions: AI’s aggregate employment impact is likely small so far; recent graduates face a tougher market that AI may be dampening in fields like software and customer service; productivity effects are mixed but generally positive, disproportionately helping less-experienced workers; firm adoption is accelerating but concentrated in tech and finance; and early evidence is far from the last word.
shortDescription: Stanford SIEPR brief separating AI-jobs hype from evidence: small aggregate employment effect so far, a tougher entry-level market, uneven firm adoption.

title: Tabular Foundation Models and the Unity of Economic Behaviour (arXiv)
author: Victor H. Aguiar
description: Tests whether a single foundation model can explain economic decision-making across domains. Using a tabular foundation model, the author hides choices in one behavioral domain and recovers them from choices in other domains plus other participants’ labeled data; the model beats baselines, the advantage vanishes when choices are reshuffled, and one random-utility model trained on the learned representation performs well across risk, time, loss aversion, valuation, and social-choice tasks — evidence for a unified structure of economic behavior.
shortDescription: Uses a tabular foundation model to recover economic choices across domains, finding a single random-utility representation predicts held-out behavior.

title: How Organizations Use AI: Evidence from ChatGPT (arXiv)
author: Aaron Chatterji, David Holtz, Neel Rakholia, Prasanna Tambe, Gawesha Weeratunga
description: Analyzes ChatGPT Enterprise usage linked to worker, task, and financial data through March 2026, covering more than 1,500 organizations and 17 million messages at the six-month mark. Finds enterprise adoption growing through both new adopters and deeper engagement by existing users, higher take-up among larger R&D-focused US public firms, use across job levels with especially strong engagement from junior employees, and applications spanning writing, technical work, communication, and information synthesis.
shortDescription: Links ChatGPT Enterprise data from 1,500+ organizations to worker, task, and financial records to trace how firms are adopting generative AI.

title: Organizational Technology Ladders: Remote Work and Generative AI Adoption (arXiv)
author: Gregor Schubert
description: Uses job-posting data to show that firms which expanded remote hiring during COVID-19 subsequently adopted generative AI at higher rates. Argues this reflects an organizational 'technology ladder' in which shifts toward technical talent and complementary capabilities accelerate later AI integration.
shortDescription: Job-posting evidence that firms which shifted to remote hiring during COVID-19 later adopted generative AI faster — a technology adoption ladder.

title: I caught my students using AI to cheat in an exam — here's what universities must do to stamp this out
author: Roberto Serrano
description: A Nature World View (10 August 2026) in which Brown University economist Roberto Serrano recounts discovering widespread unauthorized AI use on a take-home exam in his welfare-economics and social-choice course — the average score fell from 96% to 48.6% once he switched to an in-person, closed-book final. He argues universities must restore a culture of academic integrity and adapt learning and assessment methods for the age of AI.
shortDescription: Nature World View: a Brown economist recounts widespread AI cheating on a take-home exam and argues universities must defend academic integrity.

title: Where is AI in GDP statistics?
author: Anton Korinek, Patrick McKelvey
description: PIIE policy brief arguing that the rapid growth of the AI economy is largely unmeasured in conventional GDP statistics, with quality-adjusted AI production in the US growing over 2,000 percent annually in 2024-2025. The authors recommend that statistics agencies begin developing AI-focused satellite accounts now to close the measurement gap before it becomes a policy problem.
shortDescription: PIIE policy brief on why the fast-growing AI economy is largely missing from GDP statistics, urging agencies to build AI-focused satellite accounts now.

title: Research Feedback in the Style of Isaiah Andrews
description: A downloadable AI "skill" — a set of instructions that direct an LLM to give advisor-style feedback on economics research (paper drafts, slides, abstracts, and draft responses to referees) in the advising style of Isaiah Andrews. Built at his request from an audited corpus of his own written and spoken feedback, with models restricted not to train on the data. It produces a short overall assessment plus specific comments anchored to exact locations in the text, including proofs and appendices. Installable as a Claude skill or usable by pasting the included files into any LLM. Announced by Jonathan Roth alongside a companion skill for Jesse Shapiro.
shortDescription: Downloadable AI skill giving advisor-style feedback on economics drafts, slides, and abstracts in Isaiah Andrews's style; use in Claude or any LLM.

title: Advising as Jesse Shapiro
description: A skill / system-prompt file that directs an LLM to give research feedback and advising in the style of Harvard economist Jesse Shapiro — handling PhD students' research questions, document feedback, talks, and ideation. It emphasizes direct, substantive, concise responses grounded in concrete existing literature rather than abstract frameworks, and defaults to short comments on structure, exposition, and ideas. Released alongside a companion Isaiah Andrews skill and announced by Jonathan Roth.
shortDescription: LLM prompt for research feedback and advising in Harvard economist Jesse Shapiro's style: direct, concise, grounded in concrete literature.

title: AI Agents and Prompt Engineering in Econometric Coding (NBER)
author: Sebastian Galiani, Federico Ariel López, Raul A. Sosa
description: Studies how LLMs generate code for econometric tasks along three dimensions: statistical software (Stata, R, Python), prompting strategy (zero-shot vs. few-shot), and level of AI autonomy (chatbot vs. self-executing agent). Moving from a chatbot to a constrained agent raises task success from 74% to 96% at roughly eight additional cents per run. Few-shot prompting helps basic chatbots far more than autonomous agents, and software choice matters for chatbots but becomes far less consequential once an autonomous agent is used.
shortDescription: How software choice, prompting, and AI autonomy affect LLM-generated econometric code; a constrained agent lifts task success from 74% to 96%.

title: Staged Access and Liability for Dual-Use Artificial Intelligence (NBER)
author: Joshua S. Gans
description: Models how regulators should combine staged (delayed or exclusive) access to a dual-use AI model with developer liability, framing a defender and an adversary searching for the same software flaws after release. Liability induces more defensive search but also makes the adversary's search harder, so staged access and liability act as complements in protection. Because defensive effort rises toward the release date, additional delay becomes progressively less productive and optimal evaluation windows are bounded; since defensive search consumes real resources, the efficient liability rate can fall below full internalisation of harm, leaving a distinct role for a timing mandate.
shortDescription: An economic model of how staged model access and developer liability interact to limit harm from dual-use AI, and why evaluation windows are bounded.

title: Stranded credentials: how a skill-signaling market absorbed generative AI (arXiv)
author: Song Yao
description: Uses Kaggle competition data spanning 2010-2026 (444,698 participations) to ask whether professional credentials still carry information about skill after generative AI. Finds credentials are informative but perishable, institution-bound, and interdependent: recent medals retain signaling power while older credential stocks decayed sharply (upload-competition medals lost 82% of their informativeness), a shift the author attributes largely to institutional change rather than to AI directly displacing skill.
shortDescription: Kaggle data (2010-2026) on whether skill credentials still signal after generative AI: recent medals inform, older stocks decayed up to 82%.

title: Governing Delegation to Generative Artificial Intelligence: Human Direction, Work-Related Orientation, and Modes of Use (arXiv)
author: Jorge Fábrega
description: Studies how delegating tasks to generative AI redistributes control between human and model, distinguishing specified delegation (human direction set before execution) from iterative coproduction (direction supplied during production). Using the Anthropic Economic Index for April-May 2026, it compares direct API traffic with Claude.ai usage and finds that work-oriented interaction is associated with more specified delegation (+2.76 points via API, +1.45 via Claude.ai), shifting attention from how much the AI executes to when human direction leaves observable traces.
shortDescription: Uses Anthropic Economic Index data to show work-oriented AI use leaves stronger traces of prior human direction, across API vs Claude.ai modes.

title: Nora — Local Privacy Layer for AI-Assisted Statistical Analysis on Sensitive Data
author: Junhyung Byun
description: Open-source (Apache-2.0) macOS app for running AI-assisted statistical analysis on sensitive data without exposing raw data to the model. The data stays on the researcher’s machine and scripts run in a network-denied sandbox; the frontier model (Claude or GPT) sees only disclosure-control–sanitized summaries while the researcher sees raw R, Stata, or Python output. Covers regression, causal inference, survival analysis and other common methods through a Model Context Protocol interface.
shortDescription: macOS app for AI-assisted stats on sensitive data — R/Stata/Python runs locally, the model sees only sanitized summaries, never the raw data.

title: Some Simple Economics of AGI (arXiv)
author: Christian Catalini, Xiang Hui, Jane Wu
description: Introduces a macroeconomic framework that models the transition to AGI as a collision between two cost curves: the exponentially falling cost of automating execution and the biologically bounded cost of human verification. Argues the binding constraint on growth becomes verification bandwidth — the capacity to validate, audit and underwrite responsibility when execution is abundant — reframing the story from skill-biased to measurability-biased technical change, and warning that when autonomous execution scales faster than verification the economy accumulates unpriced systemic risk.
shortDescription: Macro framework for AGI: as execution automates toward zero cost, human verification bandwidth — not intelligence — becomes the binding growth constraint.

title: How experience moderates the impact of AI suggestions on researchers’ perceptions of their ideas (Research Policy)
author: Matthias Tröbinger, Anil R. Doshi, Sen Chai
description: Open-access randomized experiment with 310 researchers testing how generative-AI idea suggestions affect their self-evaluation of subsequent research proposals. Experience negatively moderates AI’s effects: less-experienced researchers are more likely to adopt AI suggestions and rate their resulting ideas as more novel and impactful, while senior researchers tend to discount AI-originated ideas — with implications for how AI reshapes knowledge production.
shortDescription: Randomized experiment with 310 researchers: junior researchers adopt AI-generated ideas and rate them more novel; senior researchers discount AI suggestions.

title: Artificial Intelligence: A Literature Review of Anticipated Economic Impacts and Regulatory Responses
author: Sam Le Quesne, Kevin Counsell, Isabelle Sin
description: A New Zealand Ministry for Regulation literature review synthesising the emerging economic literature on AI and its implications for productivity, economic growth, labour markets, inequality, uncertainty, and market structure. Key takeaways: growth impacts are uncertain, distribution matters as much as growth, labour markets are the main transmission channel, markets may misdirect AI development, and effective policy should shape AI's direction (adaptive, risk-based approaches) rather than slow progress.
shortDescription: NZ Ministry for Regulation review of the economics of AI — productivity, growth, labour, inequality, and market structure — and its regulatory implications.

title: How AI Is Changing the Role of Economists
author: Innes McFee
description: Oxford Economics CEO Innes McFee reflects on what AI can already support in economists' day-to-day work, where its limits lie, and what it means for the profession. His view: AI will not replace economists but lets them refocus where they add most value — judgement, interpreting conflicting evidence, and identifying signals others miss — the skills that become scarce as information grows abundant. Notes internal uses like AI-driven quality assurance across thousands of forecasts.
shortDescription: Oxford Economics CEO Innes McFee on how AI reshapes economists' work — automating repetitive checks while judgement and interpretation grow more valuable.

title: The Wage Effects of Generative AI (SSRN)
author: José Azar, Mireia Giné, Javier Sanz-Espín
description: Estimates how exposure to generative AI has affected wages and worker mobility, using occupation-by-industry data from the Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics alongside job postings and matched employer-employee records from Revelio. Moving from the 10th to the 90th percentile of GenAI exposure is associated with a 4.9% wage decline in OEWS, with no statistically detectable change in employment; in Revelio the same comparison implies falls of 8.71% in posted wages and 10.76% in starting wages. More exposed workers make job-to-job moves significantly less often, though transitions into persistent non-employment are unchanged, and wage declines are largest among junior workers across every age group. Exposure also lowers the elasticity of separation with respect to wages, which the authors read as evidence that firms' labor market power has risen in occupations exposed to automation by generative AI.
shortDescription: Wages fall 4.9% (OEWS) and posted wages 8.71% (Revelio) moving from the 10th to 90th percentile of GenAI exposure, with junior workers hit hardest.

title: The Labor Market Effects of Generative Artificial Intelligence and Job Loss Fears (NBER)
author: Jonathan S. Hartley, Filip Jolevski, Vitor Melo, Brendan Moore
description: Fields a survey measuring US workers perceptions of AI-related job-loss risk and AI adoption (mid-to-high 30% by end of 2025). The average worker believes there is a 20% chance of losing their job to generative AI within two years, but a continuous-treatment difference-in-differences design finds these fears are not borne out: job postings and layoffs in more exposed occupations show no statistically significant response to AI diffusion, and exposure is associated with small positive wage effects. Presented at the NBER Summer Institute 2026 Digitization and AI meeting.
shortDescription: Survey: the average US worker sees a 20% chance of AI job loss within two years, yet exposed occupations show no drop in postings or layoffs.

title: Will AI Intensify or Weaken Market Competition? (FRBSF)
author: Hamid Firooz, Sylvain Leduc, Zheng Liu
description: A San Francisco Fed working paper studies how AI affects market competition in a general-equilibrium model with heterogeneous firms and variable markups. It finds a non-monotonic relationship between AI adoption and industry concentration: at low adoption, large incumbents that adopt AI gain share, but as adoption diffuses, entry of new and smaller adopters erodes incumbent dominance and lowers concentration. The calibrated model implies concentration will likely fall as AI adoption rises above current levels, the AI-markup link depends on whether adoption is demand- or supply-driven, and a modest 3% revenue subsidy for AI adopters maximizes social welfare.
shortDescription: SF Fed model finds a non-monotonic link between AI adoption and industry concentration; a modest 3% AI revenue subsidy maximizes welfare.

title: A Research Agenda for the Economic Futures Research Fund
author: Anthropic
description: Anthropic commits $200 million to support external research on preparing society for AI economic impacts, and lays out a research agenda across five priority areas: shaping AI workplace effects, equipping workers for transitions, modernizing income support, building worker stakes in AI-driven gains, and evaluating public investments. Eligible applicants include accredited universities, independent research institutes, policy organizations, and experienced nonprofits, with typical project funding of roughly $5-30 million.
shortDescription: Anthropic $200M fund and research agenda on AI economic impacts across five areas; open to universities, research institutes, policy orgs and nonprofits.

title: AI RCTs are booming – to be useful they must evolve
author: Oliver Hanney, Tim Ohlenburg, Sharif Kazemi, Joseph Levine, Shahrukh Wani
description: Using the AEA RCT Registry and RIDIE, the authors document a fast-rising share of AI-related randomised trials in economics — on track to be one in five, up from one in thirty in under four years — spurred by new funding such as Anthropic's Economic Futures fund and J-PAL calls. They argue that randomising a rapidly evolving, widely adopted technology poses distinct challenges (iteration speed, control-group definition, generalisability, scale) and offer concrete proposals to make the coming wave of AI RCTs durable, generalisable and policy-relevant.
shortDescription: AI-related RCTs are on track to be 1 in 5 economics trials; the piece maps the boom and proposes fixes to keep the studies durable and policy-relevant.

title: The Measurement Revolution? Credible Measurement and Inference in the Age of AI (arXiv)
author: Melissa Dell, Ashesh Rambachan
description: A review of how AI is reshaping economic measurement by cheaply converting unstructured text and images into structured variables — and the new challenge this creates, since researchers must now choose among multiple plausible AI-generated measures that can yield divergent findings. The paper identifies three pipeline stages where AI intervenes (discovery, construct definition, observation), argues for validation anchored to explicit criteria rather than informal 'reasonable proxy' claims, and shows how validation samples enable sound inference despite arbitrary AI prediction bias.
shortDescription: Dell and Rambachan on doing credible economic measurement and inference with AI-generated variables, and why validation samples are essential.

title: Sophistication in GenAI Use: Field Evidence from a Large Firm (arXiv)
author: Nicholas J. Hallman, Zachary T. Kowaleski, Anu Puvvada, Jaime J. Schmidt
description: Analyzing 713,564 prompts from nearly 4,000 back-office workers across 15 functional areas over eight months in 2025, the authors measure how 'sophisticated' employees' generative-AI use is. Senior employees exhibit more sophisticated use, and sophistication varies considerably across functions (highest in Strategy, Digital Innovation, and Project Management). Strikingly, they find neither improvement in sophistication over time nor lasting gains following formal AI training, suggesting usage patterns are resistant to conventional training.
shortDescription: Field study of 713k prompts from ~4,000 workers: genAI sophistication rises with seniority, varies by function, and formal AI training yields no lasting gains.

title: Understanding AI and Productivity
author: Chad Syverson
description: In this guest essay for EIG's Agglomerations (part of the American Worker Project), the University of Chicago productivity economist weighs whether AI is behind the recent acceleration in U.S. labor productivity growth (from roughly 1.5% to 2.2% annually since mid-2022). He argues economy-wide evidence remains inconclusive: cross-sector data show only mixed correlation between AI adoption and productivity gains, but the productivity J-curve means complementary intangible investments can depress measured productivity before benefits materialize, so slow measured growth should not be read as proof that AI is not working.
shortDescription: Chicago productivity economist weighs whether AI explains recent U.S. productivity acceleration; sees inconclusive economy-wide evidence and a likely J-curve lag.

title: What Work Does Generative AI Do? (NBER)
author: Alexander Bick, Adam Blandin, David J. Deming, Tyler R. Schumacher
description: A nationally representative survey builds the first task-level generative-AI adoption indexes across occupations. It finds adoption is widespread but shallow — genAI is used across many occupations and tasks, yet within most of them fewer than half of workers adopt — with large variation among workers in similar roles.
shortDescription: First task-level genAI adoption indexes from a US survey: use is widespread but shallow, varying sharply even within the same occupation.

title: Designing AI-Augmented Peer Review (NBER)
author: Joshua S. Gans
description: Models how journals should integrate AI-generated manuscript assessments into peer review. Sharing an AI assessment with reviewers can reduce the independent information editors obtain; giving it to only one of two reviewers may better preserve human investigation, and competing policies can be tested via randomized experiments on reviewer disagreement.
shortDescription: A model of how journals should fold AI manuscript assessments into peer review without crowding out independent human judgment.

title: CentaurBench: Benchmarking LLM Capabilities on Augmenting vs. Automating Real-World Work Tasks (NBER)
author: Pattaraphon Kenny Wongchamcharoen, Kris Gulati, Min Min Fong, Abhishek Nagaraj
description: Introduces a benchmark that separately measures whether an LLM automates a task versus augments a lower-capacity worker model across seven real-world tasks. Rankings across the two regimes are only modestly correlated — the automation winner loses on augmentation in five of seven tasks — showing automation skill does not predict how well a model assists people.
shortDescription: A benchmark separating LLM automation from augmentation: the best automator often makes a poor assistant across seven real-world tasks.
